topic: Generics: in/out variance, star projection & where

questions.question: What happens when you compile this code?
options: Compile error: `MutableList` is invariant, so `MutableList<String>` isn't a `MutableList<Any>`
It compiles, but `anys.add(1)` throws `ClassCastException` because the list only holds `String`s
It compiles and runs, leaving `strings` as `[a, 1]`
Compile error only on `anys.add(1)`, because `1` is not a `String`
questions.explanation: Generic types are invariant by default, and `MutableList<E>` both reads and writes `E`, so the assignment itself is rejected. If it were allowed, `anys.add(1)` would sneak an `Int` into a list of strings, which is exactly what invariance prevents.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `map` is a generic function with its own type parameter `R`: the first call produces a `Box<Int>` holding 42, and the second a `Box<String>` holding "v=42". `b.value` is that string, not the box itself.

questions.question: A `List<String>` can be passed where a `List<Any>` is expected, because Kotlin's read-only `List` is declared as `List<out E>`.
questions.explanation: `out E` makes `List` covariant: it only produces `E` values, so a list of strings is safely a list of `Any`. `MutableList<E>` has no `out`, which is why the same assignment fails for it.

questions.question: In `interface Comparable<in T>`, what does the `in` modifier tell the compiler?
options: `T` is only consumed, so a `Comparable<Number>` can be used as a `Comparable<Int>`
`T` is only produced (returned), so a `Comparable<Int>` can be used as a `Comparable<Number>`
`T` is reified and available at runtime
questions.explanation: `in` marks a type parameter as contravariant: it appears only in input positions like `compareTo(other: T)`. Something that can compare any `Number` can certainly compare `Int`s, so the subtyping is reversed. Producing values is what `out` is for.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The upper bound `T : Comparable<T>` is what lets the body use `>`. Strings compare lexicographically, so "banana" beats "apple", and 7 > 3.

questions.question: Declaring `fun <T : Any> put(value: T)` stops callers from passing `null`, whereas a plain `fun <T> put(value: T)` would accept `null`.
questions.explanation: A type parameter with no bound has the implicit upper bound `Any?`, so `T` can be inferred as a nullable type. Bounding it with `T : Any` restricts it to non-null types.

questions.question: `ListAdapter` is declared as `abstract class ListAdapter<T, VH : RecyclerView.ViewHolder>`. What does the `VH : RecyclerView.ViewHolder` part guarantee?
options: The type argument for `VH` must be `RecyclerView.ViewHolder` or a subclass of it
`VH` is covariant, so a `UserAdapter` is also a `ListAdapter<User, RecyclerView.ViewHolder>`
`VH` is erased to `Any?` and can be any class
The ViewHolder class is created automatically by reflection
questions.explanation: `VH : RecyclerView.ViewHolder` is an upper bound: the compiler rejects any type argument that isn't a `ViewHolder` subtype, and inside the adapter `VH` can be used as a `ViewHolder`. A bound says nothing about variance; `VH` is still invariant.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Because `T` is declared `out` and only appears as a return type, `Producer<Cat>` is a subtype of `Producer<Animal>`, so the call compiles. Without `out` it would be a type mismatch, since generic classes are invariant by default.

questions.question: Why does this class fail to compile?
options: A `var` also has a setter taking `T`, putting an `out` type parameter in an input position
Type parameters can't be used in constructor parameters of a class that declares them `out`
`out` type parameters must have an explicit upper bound
`out` can only be used on interfaces, not classes
questions.explanation: A `val value: T` would be fine, because a getter only produces `T`. A `var` also generates `setValue(T)`, which consumes `T`, so the compiler reports that `T` is declared `out` but occurs in an invariant position.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `sortedWith` takes a `Comparator<in T>`, so a comparator of any supertype of `Dog` is accepted. The list is then sorted by name in ascending order.

questions.question: Given `fun process(items: MutableList<*>)`, which of these lines compile inside the function? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `MutableList<*>` means a list of some unknown type. Reads come back as `Any?`, and members that don't mention `E`, like `size` and `clear()`, work. You can't `add` anything, because the compiler can't prove the value fits the unknown element type, and a read is not a `String` without a cast.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Elements of a `List<*>` are statically typed `Any?`, but `v::class` gives each value's actual runtime class. Only the static type is `Any?`; the objects keep their real types.

questions.question: Which call does NOT compile?
questions.explanation: With `where`, `T` must satisfy every bound at once. `Int` is `Comparable<Int>` but not a `CharSequence`, so it fails. `String` satisfies both, and an empty `List<String>` is still fine, because bounds are checked on the type, not the contents.

questions.question: Java's `List<? super Integer>` corresponds to Kotlin's `MutableList<out Int>`.
questions.explanation: `? super T` is a consumer wildcard and maps to Kotlin's `in T`, so the right equivalent is `MutableList<in Int>`. `? extends T` is the producer wildcard and maps to `out T`. That's PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `Array<T>` is invariant, but the use-site projection `Array<out Any>` lets an `Array<Int>` be passed in as long as the function only reads from it. All three elements are copied, and `joinToString()` uses ", " with no brackets.

questions.question: `LoginState` is a data class that does NOT implement `UiState`. What happens with `LoginViewModel`?
options: Compile error: `LoginState` is not within the upper bound `UiState`
It compiles, and `S` silently falls back to `UiState`
It compiles but throws `ClassCastException` when `state` is first collected
It compiles with only an unchecked-cast warning
questions.explanation: Upper bounds are checked at compile time on every type argument, so `BaseViewModel<LoginState>` is rejected until `LoginState` implements `UiState`. That's the point of the bound: the base class can rely on `S` being a `UiState`.

questions.question: Why can a single `object Loading` be returned from a function whose return type is `Result<User>`?
options: `Nothing` is a subtype of every type, and `out T` makes `Result<Nothing>` a subtype of `Result<User>`
`Nothing` is erased to `Any` at runtime, so the compiler accepts any `Result` as a return value
Sealed classes skip type-argument checks for their own subclasses, since all of them are known at compile time
`object` declarations are generic over every `T` automatically
questions.explanation: `Nothing` is the bottom type, and with `out T`, `Result<Nothing>` becomes a subtype of `Result<X>` for every `X`. Without `out`, `Result` would be invariant, and you'd need `Loading` to be a class created separately for each `T`.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile error: T is declared out but occurs in in position
questions.explanation: `@UnsafeVariance` turns off the variance check for that parameter, which is how the stdlib's `List.contains` takes an `E` despite `out E`. `contains` only compares values with `equals`, so passing an `Int` to what is really a list of strings just returns `false`. Nothing gets cast.

questions.question: Given `fun fill(dest: MutableList<in Int>)`, which statements are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `in Int` accepts any list whose element type is a supertype of `Int`, so you can safely add `Int`s. What you read back could be any such supertype, so it's only `Any?`, not `Int`. `Long` is not a supertype of `Int`, so a `MutableList<Long>` is rejected.

questions.question: `Square` implements `Comparable<Shape>`, not `Comparable<Square>`. What does this print?
options: Compile error: Square is not Comparable<Square>
questions.explanation: `Comparable` is declared `Comparable<in T>`, so `Comparable<Shape>` is a subtype of `Comparable<Square>`, and `T = Square` meets the bound. In Java you'd need `T extends Comparable<? super T>` for this. The squares have areas 4 and 9, and the larger is returned.
